title: Odisha: Five baby orangutans found in India forest spark trafficking investigation
description: Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India's eastern state of Odisha, far from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into h
body: Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India's eastern state of Odisha, far from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there.Photographs and videos widely shared online show the young apes sitting together on the forest floor and eating bananas, thousands of kilometres from the tropical rainforests where they belong.Orangutans are not native to India. The critically endangered apes are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia.Odisha's forest minister has said investigators are examining whether the animals were trafficked into the country by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway.The orangutans were rescued early on Tuesday in Balasore district after local people spotted them and alerted forest officials.They were given first aid before being taken to Nandankanan Zoological Park in the state capital, Bhubaneswar, where they are in quarantine and being monitored.Balasore District Forest Officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar told the BBC that the animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and may have been transported there by road."The five animals were found in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, near the West Bengal border," he said."The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and is not a dense forest. It is also close to a state highway."The Odisha government has also reportedly asked India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate. Police, forest officials and a special task force are involved in the inquiry.

schema.headline: Odisha: Five baby orangutans found in India forest spark trafficking investigation

title: Family of murdered teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
description: The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised
body: The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer.Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter. In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old. Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times."At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday.They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life".In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard.  Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security. Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times, external reported.In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty.In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution."If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney.Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year.  Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence"."We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said. His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit.

schema.headline: Family of murdered teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial

title: Gambia's President Adama Barrow urges calm after violent blackout protests
description: The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electric
body: The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours."When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month. The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal.The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand.Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts.Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Westfield area as they moved towards the headquarters of the national electricity company, Nawec, with some chanting. "Barrow must go". Protesters also gathered outside the vice-president's residence in Farato, where banners at an office of Barrow's ruling National People's Party were damaged.The unrest comes just months before a presidential election expected in December, in which Barrow is seeking a controversial third term.In a televised address on Tuesday night, Barrow acknowledged the hardship caused by the blackouts but warned protesters against damaging public infrastructure, saying it would only worsen the disruption and divert money towards repairs."Let us not destroy in a moment of anger what we suffered so long to gain," he said.The president admitted there had been shortcomings in the government's planning, power generation and maintenance systems, calling the resulting outages "a national security issue" and an "emergency". "I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night," the president, promising that supplies would improve by the end of October.He said a new 24-megawatt generating unit was being installed at the Brikama power station and would be commissioned by the end of next month.A contract has also been awarded for a 50MW solar power plant in Soma, although no completion date was given."For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," Barrow added. The president visited facilities for the national energy utility on Tuesday morning and promised that The Gambia would receive new generators this week. Gallo Saidy, the Nawec chief, also appealed for patience, saying reduced electricity imports from the regional grid had contributed to the shortages.He said lower rainfall this year had reduced the electricity available through the regional network."We are aware of the frustration and constraints that the Gambian people have," he said. "We are just asking The Gambian people to give us a little bit of time and patience."Nawec had warned in August that unusually high temperatures had driven a surge in electricity demand, while a technical problem had also affected a major generating unit supplying imported power.

schema.headline: Gambia's President Adama Barrow urges calm after violent blackout protests

title: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
description: Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered t
body: Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show.The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx.On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards.Sánchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July.At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence".The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July]  at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades."It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity.The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on Sánchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings.Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident.However, Sánchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity.Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected".But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim."They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party.Jorge Buxadé, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that Sánchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes".The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available. Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have forseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30".A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response".Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing."The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information."

schema.headline: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge

title: Europe's royalty pay respects to King Harald V in Norway
description: Dozens of European royals and heads of state, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings, have paid their last respects to King Harald V in
body: Dozens of European royals and heads of state, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings, have paid their last respects to King Harald V in Oslo.Thousands of people lined the route during a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday afternoon, nearly two weeks after the king died aged 89.After the ceremony and burial, the Norwegian royal family, including the new King Haakon, his wife Queen Mette-Marit, and his mother and Harald's widow Queen Sonja greeted crowds from the palace balcony.A minute's silence was also observed throughout the country. Harald, who was seen as a popular, modernising figure, was on the Norwegian throne for 35 years.After 13 days of national mourning, the day began on Wednesday with ceremonial troops assembling at Akershus Fortress, the medieval castle where Harald was later laid to rest.A procession then took place, with Haakon, his sister Princess Märtha Louise and his children Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus, following the late king's coffin on foot.Mette-Marit, who recently underwent a successful lung transplant, and Sonja, 89, followed in a car.

schema.headline: Europe's royalty pay respects to King Harald V in Norway

title: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant
description: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artificial intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetim
body: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artificial intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe. Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer."Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. "However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples."It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements. "That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade."With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities. He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres. He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space. "We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here."I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

schema.headline: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant

title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on
description: Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John Resta and his wife SylviaByAlice CuddyThe US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal ac
body: Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John Resta and his wife SylviaByAlice CuddyThe US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out.Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back.The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family.On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center."After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind.Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious".A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted.Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants.The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges.Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028.But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial."My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said."Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A tribute in light above the New York City skyline, at the 2024 anniversary Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims.Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about."I want to concentrate on the memories," he said.  "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'."Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died."They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones."Image source, FBIImage caption, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed as he appeared on the FBI's Most Wanted websiteMohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda.He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z".But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse".He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial.Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case."Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University.She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions.Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John and Sylvia Resta on their wedding dayJohn Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case.The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well."During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, President George W Bush on Air Force One after the attacksRelatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice."If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts."Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial.The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm.Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing.Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency.Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions."My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are.  I just want them convicted," he said.Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal."It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said.Image source, Brett EaglesonImage caption, Brett Eagleson was 15 when his father Bruce was killed Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there."My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial."With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event"."I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended."When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year.Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in"."If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained.As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo."It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.

schema.headline: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on

title: Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree
description: The mother of a black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Jackson, Mississippi, has told the BBC she is still waiting for answers from o
body: The mother of a black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Jackson, Mississippi, has told the BBC she is still waiting for answers from officials more than a month later.Her demands have been echoed by a community in the southern US state that has been left shocked and angry.After weeks of silence, police on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that they were investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, 29, as a potential homicide - while clarifying that her official cause of death has yet to be confirmed.Authorities discovered Fortune's body on 3 August, hanging from a tree in the lot of an abandoned home.Local concern over her death has been heightened by the fact that the state has a dark history of racial violence and lynchings.The majority-black city has been left on edge. As the question lingers as to how Fortune died, petitions online signed by tens of thousands of people have called for more transparency, and members of US Congress have asked for federal intervention."It's making me angry," Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, said. "What is the hold up?"Spivey described desperate attempts to understand the status of the investigation and how multiple enquiries to police had gone unanswered.The first update she had received from authorities in weeks came in a public city meeting on Tuesday evening as Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney discussed the case and said the department "has been investigating this case from day one as a homicide".Brackney, in a statement to the BBC, elaborated and said the department always treats any pending death case as a "potential homicide" so that crucial evidence is not lost as police wait on autopsy results.The department, though, had only previously described the case as a death investigation.Tuesday's statement from Brackney said "we are conducting the investigation at the highest appropriate level while we await the medical examiner's findings", which would include an official cause and manner of death.The medical examiner's office said it would not comment on the pending case.Spivey last saw her daughter alive on 26 July, when Fortune had travelled from Mississippi, where she had lived for roughly the last decade, to Kentucky, where Spivey lives, for a family reunion.The next time she saw her daughter - in a funeral home, days before her burial - she could barely look at her body."I didn't look straight at her. Her daddy did," she said. "I kind of looked from the side."Spivey remembered their last conversation. "She was talking about, you know, maybe even coming home," she explained.Fortune's death has left the community concerned that racial violence in Mississippi could be on the rise again. And in the absence of concrete details about the case, their suspicions are left to fester.Fortune's death was the third incident in Mississippi in less than a year where police found someone dead and hanged from a tree.The other two bodies - one black male, one white - were discovered in September 2025, on the exact same day.Both were ruled a suicide, though the mother of one of the deceased - Trey Reed - contests those findings.Fed-up residents have launched an online petition, which has gathered more than 50,000 signatures, for an independent investigation into the state's chief medical examiner, Dr Staci Turner, over the handling of a recent spate of cases involving people of colour. Another petition asks for the FBI to launch an investigation into Fortune's deathThe BBC has asked Turner for comment.Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes has also expressed concerns about the police investigation, saying he'd been outside the home where Fortune was thought to have lived multiple times and has never seen officers."All cases are important, but this one - a hanging in Mississippi - should rise to the top of the food chain," Stokes said.He told the BBC he sent letters to both federal prosecutors at the Mississippi US attorney's office and the FBI weeks ago, urging that the investigation was "in dire need of assistance". He has yet to hear back from either."Nothing from nobody," Stokes said. "It's like nobody cares."The BBC has reached out to the Mississippi US attorney's office and the local FBI office for comment.US Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett has similarly requested federal intervention. In a letter to the US Department of Justice, she asked for an investigation into recent deaths in Mississippi - including that of Tasia Fortune - calling them "possible cases of modern-day lynchings". She cited the state's "appalling historical reputation of violent terrorism against black Americans".In addition to Mississippi, there have been multiple other cases nationally of black Americans found hanged from trees, including four in North Carolina this year alone. Three were ruled a suicide. An autopsy is pending for the fourth death.The BBC has reached out to the justice department for comment.Stokes is clear that he does not know whether Fortune's death was a lynching, or whether race played a part at all. Nor does he care. He just wants answers.Brandon King, president of the student National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) chapter at nearby Jackson State University, said the mystery of Fortune's death, combined with minimal updates from police, has led him and others to be "extra cautious" around campus.The feeling, King said, was that "hey, you could be next. This is in Jackson. This is in your backyard".The thought is extra worrying, he continued, because "this is supposed to be the capital. This is where I'm supposed to feel the most safe".As for Spivey, she cried before heading to a funeral home for her daughter, dreading having to fill out a death certificate and decide whether to cremate or bury her firstborn child.She wanted to cremate her daughter but decided, in the end, for a burial. She said she was holding out hope there would be updates in the investigation, which might mean needing to exhume her corpse.

schema.headline: Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree

title: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games
description: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who hav
body: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who have now returned to the UK, were not working royals.A report in The Times newspaper quoted the general's concerns about the "Harry-Meghan nonsense", suggesting this was the background to the decision."In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," said the general in an overnight post."We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval."However, royal sources have said that the King encourages all projects which support wounded service personnel.A spokesman for the Invictus Games said they had not received any official information about a potential withdrawal and have been seeking clarification from their contacts in Uganda.Among other posts on X from General Kainerugaba on Thursday was one that read: "I consider myself the most handsome, most daring and glorious Commander who ever lived."There was also a series of angry messages about other generals who had danced without his permission.The participation of Uganda in the next games, to be held next year in Birmingham, was announced in July, when Prince Harry was in London promoting the sports event, which celebrates the resilience and rehabilitation of wounded military men and women.Uganda had become the 26th country to take part in the games.

schema.headline: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games

title: Google to fund Finnish AI with €13bn investment and nuclear power pact
description: Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in th
body: Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in the country's AI infrastructure, the company announced.The US tech giant said the package would fund three new data centres, expand an existing site and support energy projects to power growing demand for AI services."This is Google's largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure," the company said on Wednesday."Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths," Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.As part of the deal, Google signed a 22-year contract with Finnish utility Fortum to buy up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear power plant.Earlier this week, TikTok announced a $1bn investment in Finland to build a new data centre in Kouvola, pointing to the country's "strong digital infrastructure, clean energy mix, robust data governance and skilled tech talent".    Finland has emerged as an attractive location for data centres because of its cool climate, plentiful low-carbon electricity and relatively uncongested power grid. The colder temperatures can reduce the energy needed to cool facilities packed with computer servers.Technology companies are racing to secure power supplies as the AI boom drives demand for vast networks of data centres.The Google investment is expected to support more than 37,000 jobs during construction and boost Finland's GDP by €3.6bn a year, according to Google. Construction is set to take place in 2027 and 2028."The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo added. "Deepening our collaboration with Google will deliver lasting benefits for both parties."Google will build new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, while expanding its existing facility in Hamina, which it established after converting a former paper mill in 2009.The infrastructure will help support products such as its AI chatbot Gemini, alongside services including Search, Maps and YouTube.Google said the investments also covered "clean energy projects, and dedicated nature and community funds to support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development"."Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland," said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google."This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives," she added.Earlier this year, Google's parent company Alphabet raised its global spending plans to as much as $205bn as it sought to expand computing capacity for AI services.The agreement with Fortum provides long-term financial certainty for the Loviisa plant, which currently generates about 10% of Finland's electricity.Fortum said Google's commitment would support an investment programme aimed at extending the life of the nuclear station and increasing its generating capacity.

schema.headline: Google to fund Finnish AI with €13bn investment and nuclear power pact

title: Trump gave $45,000 cash gifts to Natalie Harp and two other aides, public records show
description: President Donald Trump gave sizable cash gifts to four White House staffers, including $45,000 (£33,000) to his close aide Natalie Harp, financial dis
body: President Donald Trump gave sizable cash gifts to four White House staffers, including $45,000 (£33,000) to his close aide Natalie Harp, financial disclosures released by his administration show.Two staff members got the same amount as Harp, while his longtime aide and director of Oval Office Operations, Walt Nauta, received $22,000. No other White House staffer has declared any gifts from the president, the documents show. Federal employees are prohibited from receiving outside compensation for their duties.The White House has described the gifts as personal in nature, unrelated to the staffers' work and legal under US law. In a statement provided to the BBC, a White House official said that the president "has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector"."The gifts at  issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals' official government duties, and are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards," the official added. The cash gifts, totalling $157,000, are marked as a "cash gift for the holidays" for Nauta, Harp and two other officials: communications advisor Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris, a White House aide who serves as Trump's executive assistant. The White House did not answer a separate query from the BBC on why the other 91 listed staff members - including other top aides and First Lady Melania Trump's top advisors - did not receive gifts. The four recipients of the cash gifts are among those widely considered as close to the US president. Harp, 35, is among Trump's longest-serving and most loyal aides. She is often trusted with typing out his frequent Truth Social posts, among other responsibilities. Last month, she was thrust into the national spotlight after she was named as one of a small number of people who stayed with Trump as he secretly swapped planes leaving Turkey last month. Nauta, a US Navy veteran, has also long been at Trump's side. He served as a White House military valet to the president in his first term, and later joined him as an assistant at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida after he left office. In June 2023, he was indicted alongside Trump on charges that he mishandled national security documents. The case was ultimately dismissed. The third recipient, Margo Martin, is well known for documenting Trump's activities on social media. While the final recipient, 26-year-old Chamberlain Harris, officially serves as the president's executive assistant. In February, she was also appointed to the US Commission of Fine Arts which oversees the construction of the White House ballroom and other Trump-directed projects in Washington. Cassandra Burke Roberston, a law professor and director of the Center for Professional Ethics at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, told the BBC that "it's not an easy call" to say whether the cash gifts were ethical or not."If it were compensation, it's not allowed," she said. "Of course, that's where the administration's argument comes in, that it's a social gift done out of friendship. Not compensation." Additionally, Robertson said that even if legal, the gifts - along with recent controversies involving prediction markets and cryptocurrencies - could raise eyebrows among the public."It does add to a generalised perception of really rampant conflicts of interest," she said.There are no other known instances of a serving US president giving cash gifts to staffers at the White House. Many presidents, however, have given souvenirs or personal mementos to staff. President Barack Obama, for example, gave former press secretary Robert Gibbs a framed necktie that he had once borrowed ahead of the Democratic National Convention in 2004.

schema.headline: Trump gave $45,000 cash gifts to Natalie Harp and two other aides, public records show

title: Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules
description: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has signed a decree which eases restrictions on people carrying legal firearms in public. De la Espriella
body: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has signed a decree which eases restrictions on people carrying legal firearms in public. De la Espriella, who during his campaign for the presidency promised to take an iron-fist approach to crime, said it was "not right that criminals are armed to the teeth while decent people can't defend themselves".The decree lifts a suspension that had been in force for a decade, which meant that even those in possession of a permit to carry guns could not do so without additional authorisation.  De la Espriella insisted that the decree would not create a free-for-all and that tight controls over who can own a gun would remain in place. While signing the decree, the president said he had made good on his campaign promise: "A man's word is his honour, and I have honour, that's why I keep my word."The restriction on carrying legal guns in public was brought in by the then-President Juan Manuel Santos in December 2015. It was originally meant to be a temporary measure, aimed at improving security during the Christmas and New Year festivities.But the suspension was extended yearly by Santos and two subsequent presidents from opposing sides of the political spectrum: conservative Iván Duque and left-wing Gustavo Petro.Under the law, even those with a permit to carry a gun could not take it out of their homes unless they applied for - and were granted - additional authorisation. De la Espriella has insisted that his decree has removed a restriction which had never been meant to be permanent. According to Spanish newspaper El País, the decree will affect almost 700,000 people in Colombia who are already in possession of a legal permit to carry a gun.They will now be able to take their registered gun out of their home, provided their permits remain up to date.Green Alliance Party Senator Ariel Ávila described the move as a "grave error", arguing that legally held guns would end up in the hands of criminals.Ávila insisted that it created an ethical dilemma, as it should only be state forces that carry guns and act as guarantors of people's security. De la Espriella insisted that the measure would not negatively affect security in the country and said forces were targeting those holding illegal guns and had seized more than 15,000 firearms so far this year.Most of them, according to de la Espriella, belonged to members of breakaway factions of the Farc rebel group and the Gulf Clan criminal gang.

schema.headline: Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules

title: White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern
description: The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use
body: The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness.The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website. On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously".The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown."At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game."To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community."The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder.Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website."Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall.Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake.

schema.headline: White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern

title: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border
description: Two people died when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.The Starokozach
body: Two people died when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.The Starokozache crossing was shut after the overnight attack. Images from the scene show several burnt-out cars amid the debris.In Kyiv, a woman was killed and 14 people, including two children, were injured after a Russian drone hit a nine-storey building, officials said, while in Sumy three people died after a drone struck a shopping centre.In Russia, officials said four people, including a child, were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, while a drone hit an industrial facility in the Arctic city of Novy Urengoy.In the north-eastern city of Sumy, 20 people were also injured in the attack on the shopping mall on Wednesday evening, regional head Oleg Hryhorov said. He said efforts to deal with the aftermath were ongoing.Russia and Ukraine recently stepped up long-range strikes, despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.Zelensky renewed calls for international support in the wake of the attack at the Starokozache road crossing, saying "the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further".The crossing, about 500km (310 miles) south of Kyiv, was shut after the attack killed two people and injured three others, Odesa regional head Oleh Kiper said.A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to the country's foreign ministry.Moldova has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict, with Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirming that 17 drones struck Moldovan territory in August alone - more than during the whole of last year."Those who ignore or downplay these threats - and refuse to name the aggressor - are denying reality," he wrote on social media."Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility."Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Russia's defence ministry said its forces had shot down 596 Ukrainian drones overnight.Novorossiysk – in the south of the country - was hit hardest in what governor Veniamin Kondratiev described as a "massive overnight enemy drone attack".As well as the four deaths, 29 people were injured, and damage was reported to residential buildings, a church and a preschool.In Novy Urengoy, a drone attack on an "industrial facility" was repelled, regional governor Dmitry Artyukhov said. He added that the falling drone wreckage had triggered a fire but no-one had been injured.Ukraine's military said late on Wednesday that it had hit the Novourengoysky ZPKT - a major oil refinery located more than 3,000km from Ukraine's border.It said the facility's petroleum products and gas condensate were being used by Russia to continue its war effort.The strikes come a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke to US President Donald Trump by phone about efforts to end the war.The Trump administration has been pressing for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, with Kyiv saying they could take place this month. The Kremlin, however, has said it is too early to discuss a date or venue.The call followed Saturday's talks between US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Putin in Moscow, before the pair travelled to Kyiv for meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday.

schema.headline: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border

title: North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility, says nuclear watchdog
description: North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility, the head of the world's nuclear watchdog said this week, calling it a cause for "s
body: North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility, the head of the world's nuclear watchdog said this week, calling it a cause for "serious concern".The new building is part of the main Yongbyon nuclear complex, and reportedly capable of housing up to 28 centrifuge cascades used to enrich uranium.In a report published late last month, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said Pyongyang had also begun operating an expanded annex at another enrichment site.  These findings point to a steady expansion of the North's sancitoned nuclear infrastructure. The agency, which has no inspectors in North Korea since it was expelled in 2009, relies on satellite imagery for assessments."The continuation and further development of the DPRK's [Democratic People's Republic of Korea] nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," IAEA director Rafael Grossi said in a statement earlier this week. The IAEA first referred to the existence of the building in June, although Grossi had mentioned the possibility earlier in the year.  In June, the agency said that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a "newly inaugurated nuclear materials production factory" on 3 June, which it identified as the Yongbyon enrichment facility. Kim had praised the country's "greatly expanded production capacity", adding that this would "offer the possibility of carrying out larger plans", according to the agency's report. Despite running one of the poorest countries in the world, Kim spends millions each year developing a secretive nuclear arsenal. A 2022 report by a non-proliferation think-tank put this figure at $640m."What makes North Korea's nuclear programme so concerning is that many of its facilities are unknown, concealed, and thus difficult to target," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford told the BBC."Beyond Yongbyon, we know that other facilities exist: Kangson, for instance. The embeddedness of North Korea's nuclear doctrine within its foreign and domestic policy means that we should expect there to be more concealed production sites."The agency also said there were indications that operations had started at another enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, in January this year. An annex had first been constructed in Kangson in 2024, it said.It had said in April that North Korea appeared to be stepping up its ability to make nuclear bombs, saying they were monitoring the apparent expansion of Yongbyon.  The North's nuclear programme has accelerated under Kim, who has overseen a record number of missile tests. The country has fired has numerous intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) since it began testing its long-range system in 2017.The country has conducted six nuclear weapons tests so far, the last of which was in September 2017.

schema.headline: North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility, says nuclear watchdog
